name: Byzantine army of the Strategikon and the military manuals (c. 600-1071)

weightNotes.aggression: The manuals counsel against risking a pitched battle unless the odds are clearly favourable and prefer to hurt the enemy by deceit, raids and hunger (Strategikon books VII-VIII, Dennis tr.); Byzantine tactics 'mostly relied on skirmishing and ambushes' as 'a deliberate and consistent strategy' to preserve scarce men (Byzantine army page). Offensives existed (10th-century reconquest, Basil II), so not lower.
weightNotes.maneuver: A cavalry army built around mobility, ambush (Strategikon book IV) and shadowing of raiders (De velitatione, c. 970: 'skirmishing and guerrilla-type border warfare'). Kleidion (1014) was won by sending Xiphias round the mountain into the Bulgarian rear.
weightNotes.flanking: The standard cavalry array had flank guards and outflanking detachments (Strategikon book II-III); Belisarius at Dara (530) placed Heruli in ambush off his flank; Kleidion was a rear attack (Dara, Kleidion pages).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Book X is devoted to sieges and the 10th-century offensives took fortresses methodically, but the defensive system rested on holding fortified places and letting raiders exhaust themselves (Haldon 1999). Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The manual's battle order puts a second line behind the first so a beaten first line can fall back and reform, plus a rear guard and baggage guard (Strategikon II; Haldon). Manzikert (1071) shows the cost when the reserve commander, Andronikos Doukas, marched away instead (Manzikert page).
weightNotes.scouting: Scouts, spies and surprise attacks are whole books of the Strategikon (IX) and De velitatione builds the border defence on watch posts and early warning (De velitatione page). High.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.medieval low quartile 0.08. Sourced early disengagement: the Strategikon's two-line order expected the first line to fall back on the second (Dennis tr.); Manzikert 1071, the army broke with relatively low losses and many units intact (Manzikert page); Achelous 917 dissolved on a rumour of the commander's death (Achelous page). No battle gives a share at the break.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Lancer-archer cavalry with Avar-pattern kit, heavy and light infantry with bows and slings, specialised menavlatoi against enemy kataphraktoi, siege engineers (Byzantine army page). Cavalry-centred, so not higher.
weightNotes.initiative: Command was by manual and by the general; tagma and meros commanders had set drills. Thematic commanders acted on their own against raids, but battle plans were centralised. Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Strategikon book V regulates baggage trains, a fortified intermediate camp and about four days' supply; nightly fortified camps (Strategikon page; Haldon 1999, logistics chapters). Operations stayed within supply.

summary: A professional, largely cavalry army whose method was written down: the Strategikon (c. 600), Leo VI's Taktika and the 10th-century manuals. Lancer-archer cavalry deployed in two lines with flank guards and outflankers; infantry held fortified camps and defiles. Strategy was economical: avoid an even pitched battle, shadow raiders, ambush them on the way home, rely on fortified towns and the thematic system, and fight only on favourable terms or after the enemy was worn down by hunger and harassment.
whyItWorked: Doctrine matched the empire's chronic shortage of men: preserving the army mattered more than winning any one battle, and the manuals codified ambush, feigned flight and two-line cavalry tactics drawn from Avar, Persian and Arab enemies. Dara (530) and Kleidion (1014, Samuel's army trapped by an attack from the rear and thousands blinded afterwards) show the method under good commanders; the 10th-century eastern reconquest showed it could also attack.
whereItFailed: When politics split the command: at Manzikert (1071) Doukas ignored the order to cover the withdrawal, the rear guard of levies fled, and the professional core was destroyed. At Achelous (917) Simeon's Bulgarians routed the army completely. Dependence on mercenaries and court politics after 1025 eroded the thematic base that the doctrine assumed.

sources.title: Dennis (tr.), Maurice's Strategikon: Handbook of Byzantine Military Strategy (1984)
Dennis, Three Byzantine Military Treatises (Dumbarton Oaks, 1985)
Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World 565-1204 (UCL Press, 1999)
